newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia Products Outlook - Record buy props diesel.
newsitem.headline: Asia Products Outlook - Record buy props diesel.

text.p: Asia's diesel market is expected to see more support with the focus on results of the Indian tender and buying interest from local traders, industry sources said on Monday.
A record purchase last week has dispelled fears of a potential glut caused by an influx of arbitrage cargoes, they said.
Since March, more than 15 million barrels have been shipped to east Asia and India from Europe, the Mediterranean, the Middle East, Russia and the U.S.

But data released by Chinese customs on Friday showed that China imported 793,252 tonnes of diesel in March, taking its tally for the year to 2.06 million tonnes (15 million barrels). In the whole of 1996, China imported 4.6 million tonnes of diesel.
Traders noted that the volume revealed that China has not stopped importing as the market had perceived.
State-owned Indian Oil Corp (IOC) term tenders for the purchase of diesel for delivery from June 1997 to May 1998 and its spot tender to buy June cargoes, close on April 29.

But last Thursday, Hin Leong and the two traders chalked a one-day record purchase of 2.44 million barrels from a cross section of sellers many of whom were active sellers to China. On Friday, Hin Leong purchased another 300,000 barrels.
The buying spree has brought relief to arbitrage sellers who are already faced with a lack of storage space in Singapore.
Traders said inventories were brimming and they feared that China, the region main diesel importer, may not be able to absorb the excess barrels.
India had purchased 870,000 tonnes of diesel in May in 21 cargoes.
Previous consistent demand in the jet market is expected to continue in the week ahead. Traders said the physical prompt jet fuel is likely to remain around $2.00 per barrel below gasoil.
In comparison to the flurry of trade seen in the middle distillates market, activities in the fuel oil market has been thin.
Sporadic demand were seen throughout last week with an occasional spurt of buying interest seen from local traders who were moving supplies to China.

Some traders noted that the launch of SIMEX revised fuel oil futures contract early last week, has displaced some activities in the fuel oil swaps and cash market. But they said the trend may be shortlived.
They said trade is expected to pick up this week with outstanding demand from China still uncovered. China is still expected to buy 500,000 tonnes of fuel oil in May.

In the low sulphur waxy residue market, traders were sidelined while awaiting Indonesia's state-owned Pertamina's May allocation. Most had expected Pertamina to allocate around 3.6 million barrels in May, unchanged from April.
Traders expected prices to pick up, riding on North Asian summer demand for the fuel.

At the light ends, the naphtha market may see some recovery as most arbitrage cargoes were being absorbed, traders said. They said a closed arbitrage window from Europe would cap a further influx of supplies and demand is expected to increase after spring turnarounds at ethylene plants in Japan and South Korea come to a close by the end of June.
The market is also expected to be distracted by Saudi Aramco's meeting with Asian term lifters in Singapore in the third week of May to negotiate second-half 1997 lifting contracts, traders said.
The gasoline market is also expected emerge out of its current doldrums, with demand from Japan anticipated in May, after the Golden week holidays in early May, traders said.
Japan's monthly imports of four to five 100,000-barrel cargoes of reformate could be raised to as many as eight cargoes in May and June, they said.
They said trade in the coming days may still be slow as most Japanese traders would be out on holidays and only a trickle of demand was heard from Sri Lanka and Malaysia.
Traders would also be on the look out for results of Sri Lanka's import tender for late May arrival gasoline. The tender is valid until May 1.
